title: Security & Compliance: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency & Retention, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, Evidence Workflows, and Risk Exceptions
author: Asha Patel
body:
Overview:

This document codifies Redwood Inference's security and compliance controls spanning RBAC and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, Secure SDLC requirements, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence workflows, and the risk & exceptions process. It is intended to be the canonical operational reference for engineering, security, and compliance teams.

Goals:
- Protect customer data and maintain regulatory compliance.
- Reduce blast radius through least-privilege access controls.
- Ensure complete and tamper-resistant audit trails for critical actions.
- Provide predictable evidence collection and retention for audits (SOC2, ISO27001, GDPR where applicable).
- Define repeatable incident handling and risk exception processes.

1) RBAC & Authentication

Purpose:
Enforce least privilege for humans and services; ensure access is auditable and revoke-able.

Roles and ownership (summary):
- org-admin: global organizational administration. Owner: People Ops + Security (two-person approval for IAM changes).
- security-admin: manage security tooling, SIEM, incident response. Owner: Security.
- infra-admin: cloud infra operations, infra CI/CD systems. Owner: Eng-Infra.
- svc-account (machine identity): scoped to a single service; MUST use short-lived credentials where possible. Owner: service owner.
- developer: scoped to dev environments and repo-level access. Owner: respective product/engineering team.
- support: limited to customer support console and escalation workflows. Owner: Customer Success.
- auditor: read-only access to logs and compliance artifacts. Owner: Security/compliance.

Authorization model & rules:
1. Principle of least privilege: default role for new users is minimal (no console access).
2. Role binding: use group-based assignment via IAM groups (cloud and SSO groups); avoid individual role grants.
3. Just-in-time (JIT) escalation: developers request elevated access via the Access Request workflow (see section below). Timeboxed (default 4 hours) with automatic revocation.
4. Service accounts: must use workload identity (OIDC) or short-lived credentials (<= 12 hours) and have explicit owners.
5. MFA: required for all human accounts with console or privileged access.
6. Passwordless SSO is preferred; all sessions are logged and session durations limited per risk tier.

Access request & approval workflow (numbered):
1. Requestor files an access request in the Access Request Jira project with scope, justification, and duration.
2. Request lands in approver queue for the resource owner and security-admin.
3. Approvers must record compensating controls if granting broader access.
4. If approved, automation issues temporary credentials or group membership for the requested window.
5. Access automatically revokes at expiry; request is closed and archived as evidence.

Periodic access reviews:
- Service owners perform quarterly access reviews for their services.
- Security runs biannual org-wide access reviews.
- Findings are tracked in the risk register and remediated within SLA (default 30 days).

2) Audit Logging & Monitoring

Objectives:
- Maintain immutable, queryable audit trails for security- and privacy-sensitive events.
- Surface anomalous behavior to SIEM and alert SRE/Security.

What we log (minimum):
- Authentication events: login, MFA challenges, token issuance/refresh, failed attempts.
- Authorization changes: role/group membership changes, policy edits, permission grants.
- Administrative actions: IAM changes, key rotations, KMS policy changes.
- Data access: read/write/delete operations against sensitive stores (S3 buckets, DBs, object stores).
- Model-serving actions: model deploys/rollouts, config changes, model version pinning.
- Infrastructure changes: Terraform apply, cluster scaling, service restarts.
- Incident workflow actions: starts/updates/closures of incident tickets.

Log pipeline and retention:
- All logs ship to the centralized SIEM (Splunk/ELK) via secure, authenticated channels.
- Hot retention (searchable): 365 days for security/audit logs.
- Warm/Archive retention: 7 years archived in WORM storage (S3 Glacier with immutability controls) for compliance evidence where required.
- Access to archived logs requires approval from Security + Compliance.

Tamper resistance & integrity:
- Logs are written with append-only settings and immutable storage policies where supported.
- Critical log sets are checksum-signed and cross-checked daily.

Alerting and SLOs:
- Mean detection latency for high-severity events: <= 15 minutes.
- Mean time to acknowledge (security-on-call): <= 30 minutes for P1/P2 alerts.

3) Data Residency & Retention

Principles:
- Data residency defaults to the customer’s selected cloud region.
- Sensitive data classification drives retention and handling rules (PII, PCI, PHI, Intellectual Property).

Classification buckets (short):
- Public: non-sensitive, can be stored globally. Retention: as business needs.
- Internal: company-internal operational data. Retention: 3 years unless otherwise specified.
- Sensitive: PII/regulated content. Retention: default 1 year; configurable shorter by contract.
- Ephemeral/Transitory: model context or transient request payloads. Retention: 30 days by default; purged after 30 days unless opted-in by customer.

Retention policy examples (table style):
| Data type | Default region | Hot retention | Archive retention | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Audit logs | customer region + central | 365 days | 7 years (archived) | Security |
| Customer request payloads | customer region | 30 days | N/A | Product/Support |
| Embeddings & derived artifacts | customer region | 90 days | Customer-specific | Product/SRE |
| Backups (DB) | region per backup policy | 90 days | 7 years | Eng-Infra |

Data residency controls:
- Customer-configurable region selections enforced at the control plane.
- Private deployment option for customers with strict residency requirements (VPC or on-prem).
- Data egress controls and DLP scanning on outbound transfers.

Deletion & legal hold:
- Deletion requests follow the Data Subject Request (DSR) procedure; service owners must attest to deletion within 30 days.
- Legal holds supersede retention; data under legal hold are moved to a restricted archive and marked in the compliance register.

4) Secure SDLC (Secure Software Development Lifecycle)

Scope:
Applies to all production-facing services, SDKs, and deployment automation.

Required gates (each must be completed and documented in PRs or release tickets):
1. Threat modeling: for new services and significant design changes (owners: product + security).
2. Static Application Security Testing (SAST): all PRs must pass SAST gates for high/critical findings to merge.
3. Dependency and SCA scanning: block merges on high-severity vulnerable dependencies; remediation plan required for medium severity.
4. Secret scanning: fail if secrets are found in commits; automated revocation workflow triggered.
5. Dynamic application security testing (DAST) and fuzzing for public endpoints pre-release.
6. Container image scanning and SBOM generation for deployment artifacts.
7. Security sign-off: Security must approve production releases for services in scope 3 (critical infra) and scope 2 (customer-facing) by checklist.

Release controls and canary policy:
- All releases follow the canary policy: 5% traffic for 30 minutes, increase to 25% for 1 hour, then full rollout if no regression.
- Automated rollout rollback on defined KPIs (error rate increase > 2x baseline, latency P95 degradation > 40%).

Vulnerability management:
- SLA to remediate critical vulnerabilities: 72 hours.
- High severity: 14 days.
- Medium: 90 days.
- Security publishes monthly vulnerability summaries to engineering.

5) Incident Response \u2014 Security Procedures

Purpose:
Provide the operational playbook for security incidents affecting confidentiality, integrity, or availability.

Incident levels and ownership:
- P1 (Security breach / active data exfiltration): Incident Commander = Security Lead + Eng-SRE lead. Executive notifications within 1 hour.
- P2 (Privilege escalation, lateral movement detected): Security lead + service owner. Notifications within 4 hours.
- P3 (Minor security misconfiguration): Service owner with Security oversight. Notifications within 24 hours.

Initial triage checklist (numbered):
1. Validate the alert and classify severity.
2. Capture volatile evidence (memory, network captures) and preserve logs.
3. Contain: isolate compromised hosts or revoke sessions/keys as needed.
4. Engage SRE and service owners to prevent cascading failures.
5. Eradicate root cause (patch, rotate keys, remove malicious artifacts).
6. Restore and validate service integrity.
7. Post-incident actions: postmortem, customer notifications (if impacted), and retrospective remediation plan.

Communications and disclosure:
- Internal incident channel: #incidents-security (restricted).
- External communications: coordinated by Legal + PR with Security.
- Regulatory notifications: Security + Legal assess regulatory thresholds (e.g., GDPR 72-hour notification).

Evidence handling during incidents:
- All evidence stored in the forensics bucket (WORM-enabled) with access logging.
- Chain-of-custody recorded in the incident ticket.

6) Compliance Evidence Workflows

Objective:
Ensure consistent collection, cataloging, and retention of evidence for audits (SOC2, ISO27001, customer audits).

Evidence owner model:
- Every control has a named evidence owner (example: access reviews -> owner = Security Operations).
- Evidence catalog maintained in Confluence with links to artifacts in the secure evidence store (S3 with restricted access).

Standard evidence types and retention:
- Policy documents (this doc and related policies): retained for life of control, reviewed annually.
- Access review records: retained 3 years.
- Change control logs (Terraform apply, release tickets): retained 3 years.
- Pen test / audit reports: retained 7 years.
- Incident reports and postmortems: retained 7 years (redacted for public sharing).

Evidence submission workflow (numbered):
1. Evidence owner uploads artifacts to the secure evidence store and updates the Confluence control entry with links and metadata.
2. Compliance automation validates presence of required artifacts and flags missing items.
3. During audits, Compliance exports the evidence package (export requires Security + Compliance approval).
4. After audit, Compliance records findings and assigns remediation actions to owners.

Audit readiness cadence:
- Quarterly internal audit rehearsal and evidence sanity check.
- Annual external audit as scheduled.

7) Risk & Exceptions Process

Purpose:
Provide a controlled way to accept temporary deviations from security policies with compensating controls and explicit approval.

When to use:
- Technical constraints that prevent immediate compliance (e.g., third-party integration requiring legacy auth).
- Timeboxed exceptions for emergency mitigation (must still follow accelerated review).

Request process (numbered):
1. Submit a Risk Exception Request form (template stored in Confluence) including: scope, risk description, compensating controls, affected assets, mitigation timeline, and rollback plan.
2. Security performs risk assessment and documents residual risk numerically and qualitatively.
3. Approval matrix:
   - Low risk: Security manager sign-off.
   - Medium risk: Security lead + service owner sign-off.
   - High risk: CISO + relevant exec approval (must include compensating controls and board notification if required).
4. Timebox and re-evaluation: exceptions expire automatically at the stated end-date unless renewed through the same process.
5. All exceptions logged in the central exceptions ledger and reviewed at monthly risk committee.

Compensating controls examples:
- Additional monitoring/alerting for the affected scope.
- Network isolation or IP whitelisting.
- Shorter credential TTLs and mandatory rotation.

8) Roles & Responsibilities (quick reference):
- Security: policy owner, incident response lead, audit evidence steward.
- Eng-Infra: implement retention, backups, and regional controls.
- Eng-SRE: monitoring, runbooks, incident mitigation.
- Product: threat modeling, customer data handling decisions.
- Customer Success: DSRs and customer-facing retention communications.
- Legal/Compliance: regulatory interpretation, external audit coordination.

9) Operational checklists and runbooks (links & examples):
- Access revocation playbook: steps to revoke user and service credentials.
- Incident containment runbook: host isolation commands, evidence collection commands, and required ticket updates.
- Evidence submission template: what to include for access reviews, change control, and penetration tests.

Appendices:
A. Fast reference \u2014 common commands and endpoints:
- Revoke SSO session (CLI): rcli iam revoke-session --user <user@example.com>
- Export audit logs (SIEM): splunk-export --query \"index=audit OR index=auth\" --start <start> --end <end> --dest s3://forensics-bucket/<ticket-id>

B. Templates:
- Risk Exception Request: (fields) requester, service, start_date, end_date, risk_description, compensating_controls, approvers
- Incident ticket template: severity, summary, timeline, containment_actions, artifacts_uploaded (links), RCA owner

C. KPIs and reporting:
- Quarterly compliance posture score (target >= 95%).
- Mean time to detection (target <= 15 minutes for critical signals).
- Percentage of production services with security sign-off before release: 100%.
